title: Holding a nation together for two thousand years: not armies, but the dietary taboos of three daily meals
dek: Eating is a ritual too frequent to evade: repeating the same meals daily embeds identity into the body more deeply than military or political power can. Jews survived two millennia of statelessness through dietary taboos alone.
why: From taboos and court ritual to McDonald's standardization: dense case studies show how eating has always been distributing status and power, with minimal digression.
who: Readers interested in social order, identity formation, and consumption hierarchies—especially those following China's ritual systems and the history of global commodity exchange.
skip: 1:11–1:14: personal anecdotes about food-seeking and rice-noodle restaurant recommendations—low information density, skippable.

points.h: Taboo content is arbitrary; drawing boundaries is essential
points.body: Jews cannot eat most dishes at a full Manchu-Han banquet—the specific content of any taboo is contingent, but drawing the line between ‘us’ and ‘them’ is inevitable. Greeks distinguished themselves from meat- and milk-eating ‘barbarians’ through wine and bread; Song people used the character 膻 (musky odor) to describe Jurchen eating lamb. The content varies, but all use the high-frequency act of eating to reaffirm identity—harder to evade than ritual worship.

points.h: Ritual distinguishes rank; one piece of meat broke the whole system
points.body: The Book of Rites says ‘ritual begins in eating and drinking’; the foundations of Zhou protocol were who could share a table, what served first, how meat was cut. ‘Ritual did not extend to commoners’ means only nobles were bound by these rules. Yet the system was fragile: when the Zhou king mistakenly gave sacrificial meat meant only for same-clan lords to Qi Huangong (an outside-clan lord), Huangong accepted gladly—ritual collapsed from the top, at this meat, before Confucius even denounced the ‘eight rows of dancers in the courtyard’.

points.h: Versailles dining: complexity without meaning becomes nobility
points.body: Louis XIV confined the nobility to Versailles to reinforce his power against commoners. The method was not to make dishes complex, but to make the act of eating complex—needlessly complex, because complexity with purpose undermines the leisure class's status. By contrast, Germany and England, with weaker centralization and smaller distance between lords and people, had no need for such display, so never developed the same level of elaborate table ritual.

points.h: Corn mattered more than chili peppers: controlling famine
points.body: Both chili peppers and corn arrived in China through Columbian exchange, but chili's path is traceable: landing first in coastal Zhejiang, then spreading in two lines west and north through the Qing to today's Sichuan, Yunnan, and Shaanxi—all within four hundred years. Corn was heavier freight: after the Kangxi and Yongzheng eras, population surged while many places could not sustain their people. Corn became staple food across much of China, directly determining ‘how few starved’.

points.h: Famine is not scarcity but outflow—grain flows out of starving regions
points.body: Economist Amartya Sen studied modern famines in Ethiopia and elsewhere, finding that most stem not from insufficient production but from breakdown in transport and distribution. More counterintuitively: the poorer a place and the more it lacks grain, the less its people can afford grain—so prices fall, and grain flows out. Starving regions export grain. After industrialization, eating became not a production problem but a systemic one.

points.h: McDonald's raised the floor of global eating to the old ceiling
points.body: With minimal variety, standardized making and delivery, McDonald's raised the global eating floor very high—nearly to yesterday's ceiling. The Big Mac became an international price-comparison currency (the Big Mac Index). Meanwhile, the ceiling moved: high-end restaurants began layering sound, light, piano music with taste, evolving toward immersion and art, while the mass market solved basic subsistence through industrial systems. Two completely separate paths.

points.h: The more abstract society becomes, the more concretely human eating needs to be
points.body: From agriculture to industry to the information age, people's interfaces have shifted from other humans to faceless systems, and alienation and loneliness follow. The core insight: the more abstract the society, the more concreteness people crave—and cooking is irreducibly concrete. Even the same bowl of noodles at the same shop, depending on whether a pinch of scallion is scattered on top, can create real disagreement and friction between two people. That friction itself is where concrete feeling comes from.

points.h: Valencians say: your paella is a betrayal
points.body: Go to Valencia and locals say: what we make is real paella—what the world knows as Spanish paella is a variant, a betrayal of the authentic local way. The Columbian era opened a process of global homogenization, but the tension between local and international persists. Local terroir raises concrete people and concrete craft—and in a world of standardization and assembly lines, that concreteness is the only door back in.

quotes.text: This taboo is actually a way of marking identity: whoever keeps this taboo is one of us, is one of our own.
And in that era, dietary taboos sustained the existence of their entire people—only through, day after day, three meals a day.

In classical China, a fundamental social order is ritual—ritual's purpose is to distinguish rank. The Book of Rites captures this well: this vast system of ritual, regulating matters great and small, says: ‘ritual begins in eating and drinking’.
So first and foremost, this is a mystery sparked by a piece of meat—not yet the ‘eight rows of dancers’; those came much later.
Complexity without meaning is what makes leisure visible—that's where status comes from.

You'd think grain scarcity would make grain expensive there. True—until people fall into such deep poverty that they lose all purchasing power. Then grain prices collapse locally, and because no one can buy it, grain flows outward. The more starving the region, the more grain leaves it.
So the more abstract the era, the more abstract society becomes, the more people crave what is concrete—and eating, cooking, is precisely an irreducibly concrete act.
What we make here is what paella really is. What you hear about around the world as Spanish paella—that's all a variation, a betrayal of what we do here.
